title: Antigen presentation and MHC
objective: Explain how MHC molecules present antigen so T cells can recognize infection.

steps.title: T cells read fragments, not whole microbes
steps.body:
A T cell can't see a whole pathogen. It sees short peptide fragments held up by **[[MHC]]** (major histocompatibility complex) molecules on cell surfaces.

- **MHC class I** is on almost all cells and shows samples of what's *inside* (so cytotoxic T cells can spot infected cells).
- **MHC class II** is on professional [[antigen-presenting cell|antigen-presenting cells]] and shows what they've *engulfed* (to helper T cells).

visual.alt: Top: an infected cell shows an internal peptide on MHC class I to a cytotoxic T cell. Bottom: a dendritic cell shows an engulfed fragment on MHC class II to a helper T cell. The T-cell receptor reads the peptide held in each MHC groove.
visual.caption: MHC I shows internal peptides; MHC II shows engulfed ones.

pairs: Displays internal peptides to cytotoxic T cells
Displays engulfed peptides to helper T cells
steps.explanation: Presentation is how the adaptive system inspects cells from the inside out, and how innate cells (which do the engulfing and presenting) hand off to adaptive ones.

steps.title: The bridge from innate to adaptive
steps.body:
A [[dendritic cell]] engulfs microbes in a tissue, travels to a lymph node, and presents the fragments on MHC class II to helper T cells. That handoff is what *starts* most adaptive responses.

So innate sensing (B1) and adaptive specificity (B2) are physically linked by antigen presentation.

steps.prompt: A virus infects a skin cell. How can the immune system tell that cell is infected?
options: It can't be detected until the cell bursts and releases the virus
It shows viral peptides on MHC class I, which cytotoxic T cells read
Antibodies slip inside the cell and bind the virus within it
Neutrophils read the cell's DNA to detect the viral infection
steps.explanation: MHC class I shows internal (including viral) peptides, letting cytotoxic T cells detect and kill infected cells, surveillance from the inside.

steps.prompt: Why does the term 'MHC' also come up in transplant rejection?
options: It doesn't; MHC has no bearing on transplanted tissue at all
MHC differs between individuals, so T cells see foreign MHC on a graft
MHC is a drug given to patients to prevent organ rejection
MHC matters only in laboratory mice, not in human transplants
steps.explanation: The 'histocompatibility' in the name is literal: MHC differences drive transplant rejection, which is how these molecules were first discovered.

flag.note: Transplant immunology is more complex; this is the core reason MHC matters there.
